title: Why Your Taste Buds Die Every 10 Days
description:
How do taste buds work, why is the tongue map a myth, and why do your taste cells get replaced about every 10 days? A simple explainer of papillae, taste receptors, the five basic tastes (sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami), why smell makes most of flavor, and the catfish with 175,000 taste buds.

Sources:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue_map

topic: Your Taste Buds Explained in Simple Words: how taste buds work and why they die every ten days
script: Your taste buds die every ten days, and nobody ever told you why. Right now, thousands of tiny sensors are tasting your own spit. So what are they, how do they work, and what about that tongue map from school? Let's start with the map. You've probably seen it. Sweet on the tip, bitter at the back, sour and salty on the sides. It's a myth. In nineteen oh one, a German scientist named David Hanig found that some spots were just a tiny bit more sensitive. Then in nineteen forty two, his graph got redrawn, and people read it the wrong way. The truth? Every part of your tongue that has taste buds can taste all five flavors. So where are the taste buds? Stick out your tongue in a mirror. Those little bumps are not taste buds. They're called papillae, and most taste buds hide inside them, along the sides of each bump. An adult has somewhere between two thousand and ten thousand taste buds. A few even live on the roof of your mouth and down in your throat. Now zoom in on one bud. It looks a bit like a tiny onion, packed with fifty to one hundred fifty taste cells. At the top there's a little opening, called a taste pore. When you eat, food dissolves in your spit, and those molecules slip into the pore. Each taste cell has receptors on its tip, like locks waiting for the right key. Sugar fits the sweet lock. Salt slips through its own little channel. When a key fits, the cell fires a signal down a nerve, and your brain says, sweet! And here's the clever part. Each of the five tastes has a job. Sweet means energy. Salty means minerals your body needs. Sour can mean unripe, or spoiled. Bitter is a warning, because lots of poisons taste bitter. And umami means protein. That fifth taste was found in nineteen oh eight, by a Japanese chemist named Kikunae Ikeda. He wondered why seaweed soup tasted so rich, and found the answer was glutamate. But taste is only half the story. Hold your nose and eat a jelly bean. You can tell it's sweet, but not what flavor it is. That's because most of what we call flavor actually comes from smell. And some animals put us to shame. A catfish can have up to one hundred seventy five thousand taste buds, all over its body. It's basically a swimming tongue. Now, back to that hook. Your taste cells work in a wet, rough place, getting scraped by crunchy food, and burned by hot soup. So your body replaces them, about every ten days. That's why a burned tongue feels normal again so fast. Every bite you take, thousands of brand new taste cells are on the job. Next time, why do some people get carsick, while others feel totally fine?
key_facts: Adults have about 2,000 to 10,000 taste buds, each with 50 to 150 taste receptor cells; taste cells are replaced roughly every 10 days (Cleveland Clinic)
Most taste buds sit in papillae (fungiform, circumvallate, foliate); a few are on the roof of the mouth and in the throat (Cleveland Clinic)
Tongue map myth: David P. Hanig's 1901 paper found only minute threshold differences; Edwin Boring's 1942 redrawn graphs were misread; all tastes are sensed across the tongue (Wikipedia: Tongue map)
Umami identified by chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 from kombu seaweed broth; the molecule is glutamate (BrainFacts)
Large catfish can have up to 175,000 taste buds, all over the body (Live Science)
